I have played, Octavius, while slender Thalia gave the measure,
and like little spiders have spun a delicate thread.
I have played: let these be the songs spoken on behalf of the Gnat,
so that the whole course of the tale may chime in sport
for the learned, and let learned men approve, though the envious be present.
Whoever stands ready to blame these jests and the Muse,
will be carried lighter than the weight of a gnat, and lighter in fame.
Hereafter my Muse will speak to you in a graver strain,
when the seasons grant me their unanxious fruits,
that songs worthy of your judgment may be polished for you.
Glory of Latona and of great Jove, golden offspring,
Phoebus shall be the prince and author of my song,
and its patron with answering lyre, whether
Arna nurtures him, drenched with the Chimaerean stream of Xanthus,

or the glory of Asteria, or where the Parnassian rock
spreads forth its horns on this side and that with broad brow,
and the sounding wave of Castalia glides on its liquid foot.
Wherefore, glory of the Pierian spring, come, sisters,
Naiads, and celebrate the god with the chorus's applause.
And you, holy Pales, to whom the rustics' coming
returns, may their care be secure that holds
the airy tendance of the groves and the greening woods:
with you as my guardian I am borne, a wanderer, among glades and caverns.
And you, for whom assurance arises from deserving pages,
venerable Octavius, glide to my undertakings,
holy boy; for not for you does my page sing of war,
the grim war of Jove, and it lays aside . . . Phlegra, the land sprinkled with Giant-blood,
nor does it drive the Centaurs against the swords of the Lapiths,

nor does the East scorch the Erichthonian citadels with fires,
nor will Athos pierced through, nor the chains cast upon the great sea
now seek belated fame in my volume,
nor the Hellespont beaten by the hooves of horses,
when Greece feared the Persians coming from every side,
but soft songs, ranging in slender verse,
driven by their own strength, rejoice to play with Phoebus as their guide.
These things, holy boy, we will record for you; for you may this
glory remain, shining, abiding through perpetual ages.
And may a place await you in the holy abode, and for you, safe,
may the life you are owed be remembered through happy years,
welcome, shining for the good. But let us be borne to our beginning.
The fiery Sun had now pierced the ethereal heights
and was shaking his bright light from his gilded chariot,

and Aurora with her rosy locks had put the shadows to flight:
the shepherd drove the she-goats from the stalls to the glad pastures,
and sought the topmost ridges of the lofty mountain,
where flowering grass clothed the open hills.
Now wandering through woods and thickets, now in the valleys
they hide their bodies, and now, swift, straying everywhere,
they cropped the greening grass with tender bite.
They clung to the rocky hollows on the lonely banks,
and the hanging arbutus is plucked from the outstretched branches,
and the dense wild-vine is eagerly sought among the thickets.
This one snatches at the high tips with cropping bite,
or of the pliant willow, or of the alder newly springing;
this one searches the tender briars of the bushes, but that one
leans over toward the shadow of its image cast in the stream.

O blessings of the shepherd, if any, with mind first taught,
disdain not the way of life of the poor man, and approve for him
dreams of luxury, unknown, his cares spurned—
cares that rend greedy minds with hostile breast.
If the fleeces, twice washed and seething with Assyrian dye,
given with Attalic wealth, do not seethe for him; if the gleam of gold
beneath the panelled ceiling of a house wrings not his greedy soul,
nor the glory of paintings, nor the gleam of gems is kept
in any service known, nor do Grecian cups
recall the chased-work of Alcon and Boethus, nor is the Indian
shell-pearl of the sea held at a price; yet with pure breast
he often stretches his body upon the tender grass,
when the flowering earth, painted through its jewelled herbs,
in spring marks out the fields, picked out with uncertain colours.

he tends the groves, for him the rustic herbs add Panchaean incense
with their varying flowers,
for him sweet rest is present, and pure pleasure
free; on simple cares he fixes his mind here, all
his senses he directs here, this care is laid to his heart,
that, content with whatever fare, he may abound in rest,
and bind his languid limbs in pleasant sleep.
O flocks, O Pans, and O most welcome vales
of the spring of the Hamadryads, by whose not-rich worship
each poet, a rival to the Ascraean shepherd,
leads an untroubled life with placid breast.
In such pursuits, while, leaning on his staff, the shepherd
drives his sunny cares, and while with no tuneful art
he modulates a solid song on his joined reed,
the heat of Hyperion stretches forth its borne-up rays,
and sets bright boundaries in the ethereal world,

where it hurls its devouring flames into either Ocean.
And now, as the shepherd drives them on, the wandering she-goats
sought again the lowest fords of the murmuring water,
which, dark-blue, lay beneath the green moss.
Now the sun had passed the middle portions of his work,
when the shepherd was gathering his dense flocks into the shades.
As soon as he saw, far off, the Delian goddess
resting in the greening grove—in your frenzy, by which once
overcome, Cadmean Agave came, fleeing the Nyctelian,
the wicked one, who, raging with unspeakable and blood-stained hands,
on the cold ridges, rested in a cavern,
the penalty afterward to come from her son's death—
here too the Pans, sporting in the green grass,
and the Satyrs and the chorus of Dryad girls
led the dance in the company of the Naiads. Not so much

did the Oeagrian hold back Hebrus lingering on its banks and the woods by his singing,
as you, goddess, they delay with their nimble dance,
glad, pouring forth many joys at your countenance.
The very nature of the place gave them a home with resounding
murmur, and refreshed them, wearied, in the sweet shade.
For first, from the sloping valley, there rose the spreading
airy plane-trees, among which the impious lotus,
impious, which drove off the comrades of the mourning Ithacan,
while it held them, captive, with its too-great sweetness as host.
But there were the trees into which, his limbs scorched, thrown
from the conspicuous chariot of horses, Phaethon had changed
the Heliades, who, having entwined their arms in tender trunks,
poured forth bright veils from their stretched-out branches.

Then there was the tree to which Demophoon left eternal
treachery for her who laments his sins: treacherous to many,
treacherous Demophoon, and now to be wept for by maidens!
This the fateful oaks accompanied,
oaks given before the seeds of Ceres' life:
the furrow of Triptolemus changed them for ears of grain.
Here the pine, brought forth as the great glory of the Argo's ship,
adorns the tall woods, shaggy through its limbs,
and seeks to touch the stars on the airy mountains.
The form of the ilex and the black, and the wept-for cypress,
and the shady beech, and the ivies binding
their arms, warn the poplar not to mourn the blows of its brother,
and they themselves climb, pliant, to the topmost crests,
and paint golden clusters with a pale-green hue.
Among them was the myrtle, not ignorant of its old fate.

But the birds, perching on the spreading branches,
pour forth sweet songs resounding through their varied strains.
Beneath these there was water flowing from the cold springs,
which, driven in light streams, sounds its placid liquid.
And on every side the voice of birds clamours upon the ears;
here they bring back plaintive notes whose bodies, swimming in the mud,
the water cherishes; the air's echo feeds the sound,
and all things resound with the shrill cicadas in their ardour.
But around, here and there, the wearied she-goats lay down,
above the high thickets, which, gently breathing,
the breeze of the murmuring wind seeks to mingle.
The shepherd, when he had rested at the spring in the dense shade,
his limbs flung down, conceived a gentle slumber,
anxious at no ambush, but slack in the grass

the leader of the flock lying down opposite. More keenly it presses on,
spreading its eyes to fix them, and snatching at the foe more often
to break him, because anyone had come to its
fords. It reckons up the arms of its nature,
it burns in mind, it rages with hissings, it thunders with its mouth,
the coil of its body is twisted with overturned bends,
bloody drops trickle everywhere along its tracks,
it bursts its throat with its breathings. As it makes ready all things,
the tiny nursling of the moisture first frightens it,
and warns it to escape death by its sting. For
where the parted eyes spread open his cheeks, gleaming,
here the old man's pupil, mature, was struck
by the light weapon, when, furious, he sprang up and sent it,
crushed, to death; from whom all
breath, scattered, departed with its sense. Then, holding grim

eyes, he looked back upon the serpent close at hand, and then,
nimble, breathless, scarcely master of his mind, he fled,
and dragged a strong trunk from a tree with his right hand.
What chance allied his aid, whether the divinity of the gods,
it is doubtful to declare, but he had strength to conquer with such a weapon
the bristling, rolling backs of the scaly dragon,
and as it struggled and foully struck back with frequent
blows, he smites its bones where the crests gird its temples.
And because he was slow, the languor of sleep removed,
unknowing as he looked, fear had blinded his limbs—
this filled his mind the less with dire dread.
When he saw it, slain, grow faint, he sat down.
And now rising Night shakes her two-yoked horses from Erebus,
and slow Vesper advances from gilded Oeta,

when, the flock driven together, the shepherd, the shadows doubling,
goes on, and prepares to give rest to his wearied limbs.
When sleep, the lighter, entered through his body,
and his languid limbs rested, slumber poured out,
the likeness of the gnat came to him, and to him,
sad at the outcome of its death, sang reproaches.
"Who," it said, "and to what fortune borne, am I forced
to undergo this bitter change? While your very life was dearer to me
than my own life, I am snatched through the void by the winds.
You, slack, refresh your pleasant limbs in rest,
snatched from foul disasters: but my shades
the gods compel to swim across the Lethean waters.
I am driven, the prey of Charon. I have seen how, blazing with torches,
all the thresholds shine in the infernal temples.

Opposite, Tisiphone, decked everywhere with serpents,
shakes at me both flames and savage lashes. Behind
is Cerberus, with mouths barking from dread jaws,
whose necks gleam pale with snakes bent back this way and that,
and the orbs of his bloody light flash with fire.
Alas, why has your gratitude departed from its duty, when
I restored you to the upper world from the very threshold of death?
Where are the rewards of piety, the honours of piety?
They have passed into empty changes; from the field has departed
that former faith of justice. I saw the dangers
of another, leaving my own fate without regard.
I am driven to a like outcome. The penalty befalls the deserving.
Let the penalty be ruin; only let the will be welcome,
let an equal duty arise. I am borne, plucking pathless ways,

pathless ways stretching far between the Cimmerian groves;
around which grim Penalties throng at the gates;
for huge Otus sits bound with serpents,
sadly beholding Ephialtes bound far off,
since once they tried to tear apart the universe.
And Tityos, Latona, mindful, anxious of your wrath
(your wrath too implacable), lies as food for the bird.
I am terrified to stand among such shades, I am terrified,
recalled to the Stygian waters. Scarcely does the last by the river
stand out, who betrayed the nectarous food of the gods,
turned to all things by the dry sense of his throat.
What of him who rolls his stone afar against the opposing mountain,
whom grief, embittering, conquers, scorned by the powers,
seeking rest with frustrations? Go, maidens,
go, you for whom the grim Erinys kindled the torches,

Persephone, opposite, urges the heroine companions
to bear opposing torches. Alcestis remains untouched
by all care, because she lingered in the savage
distress of Admetus' husbandhood in Chalcodonia.
Behold, the wife of the Ithacan, ever a glory, the daughter of Icarius,
remains, womanly glory conceived, and far off that
fierce throng of young men, the suitors, pierced through with darts.
Why, wretched Eurydice, did you draw back in such great grief?
Does the penalty of looking back still even now await Orpheus in you?
Bold indeed was he, who ever believed Cerberus gentle,
or the power of Dis to be appeasable by any man,
nor feared raging Phlegethon with its burning waves,
nor the realms of Dis sad with their veil of rust,
and the dug-out homes and Tartarus beset
with bloody night, nor the abode of Dis—not easy—without a judge,

a judge who avenges, after death, the deeds of life.
But fortune, prevailing, had made him bold before.
Now the swift rivers had stood still, and the throng of wild beasts,
following his coaxing voice, had settled in Orpheus' region;
and now the oak had moved its deepest root high
from the green earth, the rivers had stood, and the sounding woods
of their own accord snatched his songs with their greedy bark.
The Moon too, gliding with two yoked horses through the stars,
checked her steeds: and you, monthly maiden, the running
ones you held, to hear the lyre, the night abandoned.
This same lyre could conquer for you the wife of Dis,
and grant Eurydice to be led back of her own accord: it was not lawful,
it was not appeasable for the goddess of death to grant return to life.

She indeed, having found the shades too severe,
was marking the appointed way, nor did she turn within
her eyes, nor did her tongue corrupt the goddess's gifts.
But you, cruel one, you the more cruel, Orpheus.
Seeking dear kisses, you broke the commands of the gods.
Worthy of pardon was your love, welcome the sin, if Tartarus
could know it; it is grievous to remember. You await the ages of the pious,
you the band of heroes await opposite. Here too both
sons of Aeacus: for Peleus and the valour of Telamon
rejoice in the untroubled powers of their father, on whose
marriages Venus and Virtue laid honour.
Hesione carries off this one, but a Nereid loved that one.
Beside him sits the youth, the glory of an allied lot,
keen, unsurpassed, bearing back from the Argolic ships
the Phrygian fires, repelled, the throng trembling.

O who would not tell of such partings of war,
which the men of Troy saw and the Greeks saw,
when the Teucrian land streamed with much blood,
and the stream of Simois and Xanthus, near the Sigean
shores, when the wrath of savage leader Hector
thrust the Trojans, with hostile mind, against the Pelasgian ships,
ready to bring wounds, weapons, deaths, fires?
For Ida herself, the parent of fierceness, and Ida herself,
the nurse, supplied torches to her eager nurslings,
that all the shore of the Rhoetean coast might be given
to ashes, the fleets burned up, with weeping flame.
On this side, opposed against him, stood the Telamonian hero,
and with his shield interposed he gave battle, and on that side
was Hector, the highest glory of Troy, each keen
(as the crash is from a whirlwind when the lightnings strain),

this one with hands and weapons above . . . to snatch away the return; the other, protected,
strives to drive the Vulcanian wounds with his iron from the ships.
In this aspect the son of Aeacus rejoiced in honour,
and the other, because, with blood poured upon the Dardanian plains,
victorious he lustrated Troy with Hector's body.
Again they roar bitterly, because Paris slays this one, and because
the valour of this one fell, struck by the wiles of the Ithacan's arms.
Against him the offspring of Laertes bears averted looks,
and now the victor over Strymonian Rhesus and over Dolon
rejoices, exulting in the Palladium, and again he trembles
now at the Cicones, and now, fierce, he shudders at the Laestrygonian threshold.
Him rapacious Scylla, girt with Molossian hounds,
and the Aetnaean Cyclops, him the Zanclaean Charybdis

when, whether by heavenly fate or by the rising of a star,
on every side the brightness of the sky is changed, all things with winds,
all things with whirlwinds are troubled. Now the wave of the sea
contends to rise to the stars, and now from above
it threatens to seize both the sun and all the stars,
and the crash of heaven to rush down upon the lands. Here, lately rejoicing,
the host is now surrounded, anxious, by wretched fates,
and dies above the waves and the rocks of Caphereus,
or among the Euboean crags and the Aegean shores far and wide,
while the Phrygian spoil, scattered everywhere, destroyed,
all of it now floats, shipwrecked, on the watery flood.
Here other heroes sit, equal in the honour of valour,
and all are seated in the middle abodes,
all whom Rome, the glory of the great world, looks up to.

Here the Fabii and the Decii; here too is the Horatian valour,
here too the old fame of Camillus, never to die.
And Curtius, whom once, devoted, the gulf in the midst
of the city's seats consumed in the wave amid the wars.
And Mucius, prudent, who endured the burning in his body,
to whom the frightened power of the Lydian king gave way.
Here Curius, comrade of bright valour, and that
Flaminius who gave his devoted body to the flame.
By right therefore such honours, the seats of piety,
and the Scipio-leaders, by whose triumphs the devoted
walls of Libyan Carthage bristle beneath the rubble.
Let them flourish in their own praise; I am forced to go
to the shadowy lakes of Dis, bereft of the light of Phoebus,
and to suffer the vast Phlegethon, where, greatest Minos,
you separate the wicked from the pious by their bonds and seat.

Therefore, both to tell the cause of death and of life,
the savage Penalties force me with their lashes before the judge,
since you are the cause of my evil, nor are you present as a witness,
but care more bearably. Do you hear these things, unmindful?
Yet, when you have heard them, you will scatter all to the winds,
and my words will be snatched through the spreading breezes.
I depart, never to return. You, tend the spring
and the green woods of the groves and the pastures, glad."
It spoke, and sadly with its last word withdrew.
When the idleness of life dismissed him, anxious,
groaning heavily within, nor did he bear any longer
the grief poured into his senses at the gnat's death,
as much as his aged strength bestowed upon him—
yet with which, fighting, he had conquered the hostile foe—

near the stream of water, hidden beneath the green foliage,
he sets about, unwearied, to shape a place. This he marks out
into a circle, and sought again the hilt of his iron for use,
to dig the grassy earth from the green turf.
Now, mindful, carrying through the labour he had begun, his care
heaped up the gathered work, and with a great mound
of earth the tomb grew, shaped into a circle,
which round about, forming a stone of smooth marble,
he sets, mindful of his constant care. Here too the acanthus,
and the rose, growing bashful, crimson, around the circle,
and every kind of violet. Here too is the Spartan myrtle
and the hyacinth, and here the crocus brought forth in the Cilician field,
the laurel likewise, rising, the glory of Phoebus. Here the oleander,
and lilies, and the not-pathless care of the sea-rosemary,

SPRING.
COME, gentle SPRING, AETHEREAL MILDNESS, come,
And from the bosom of yon dropping cloud,
While music wakes around, veil'd in a shower
Of shadowing roses, on our plains descend.
O HERTFORD, fitted, or to shine in courts,
With unaffected grace; or walk the plain,
With INNOCENCE and MEDITATION join'd
In soft assemblage, listen to my song,
That thy own Season paints; when NATURE all
Is blooming, and benevolent like thee.
AND see where surly WINTER passes off,
Far to the north, and calls his ruffian blasts;
His blasts obey, and quit the howling hill,
The shatter'd forest, and the ravag'd vale:
While softer gales succeed, at whose kind touch,

Burst into floods of wine. The knotted oak
Shook from his boughs the long transparent streams
Of honey, creeping thro' the matted grass,
Th' uncultivated thorn a ruddy shower
Of fruitage shed, on such as sat below,
In blooming ease, and from brown labour free,
Save what the copious gathering, grateful gave.
The Rivers foam'd with nectar; or diffuse,
Silent, and soft, the milky maze devolv'd.
Nor had the spongy, full-expanded fleece,
Yet drunk the TYRIAN dye. The stately ram
Shone thro' the mead, in native purple clad,
Or milder saffron; and the dancing lamb
The vivid crimson to the sun disclos'd.
Nothing had power to hurt the savage soul,
Yet untransfus'd into the tyger's heart,

With pious toil fulfill'd, the callow young
Warm'd, and expanded into perfect life,
Their brittle bondage break, and come to light,
A helpless family, demanding food
With constant clamour. Oh what passions then,
What melting sentiments of kindly care
Seize the new parents' hearts? Away they fly
Affectionate, and undesiring bear
The most delicious morsel to their young,
Which equally distributed, again
The search begins. So pitiful, and poor,
A gentle pair on providential HEAVEN
Cast, as they weeping eye their clamant train,
Check their own appetites, and give them all.
NOR is the courage of the fearful kind,
Nor is their cunning less, should some rude foot

Indulging all to love: or on the bank
Thrown, amid drooping lillies, swells the breeze
With sighs unceasing, and the brook with tears.
Thus in soft anguish he consumes the day,
Nor quits his deep retirement, till the moon
Peeps thro' the chambers of the fleecy east,
Enlighten'd by degrees, and in her train
Leads on the gentle hours; then forth he walks,
Beneath the trembling languish of her beams,
With soften'd soul, and wooes the bird of eve
To mingle woes with his: or while the world,
And all the sons of care, lie hush'd in sleep,
Associates with the midnight shadows drear;
And, sighing to the lonely taper, pours
His idly-tortur'd heart into the page,
Meant for the moving messenger of love;

Of light, and life, and grace, and joy below!
How shall I then attempt to sing of him,
Who, Light Himself, in uncreated light
Invested deep, dwells awfully retir'd
From mortal eye, or angel's purer ken;
Whose single smile has, from the first of time,
Fill'd, over-flowing, all those lamps of heaven,
That beam for ever thro' the boundless sky:
But, should he hide his face, th' astonish'd sun,
And all th' extinguish'd stars, would loosening reel,
Wide from their spheres, and chaos come again.
And yet, was every faultering tongue of man,
Almighty Poet! silent in thy praise;
Thy matchless works in each exalted line,
And all the full harmonic universe,
Would vocal, or expressive, thee attest,

Thunders and shakes th' astonish'd country round.
Now a blue watry sheet; anon dispers'd,
A hoary mist; then gathered in again,
A darted stream aslant the hollow rock,
This way, and that tormented; dashing thick,
From seep to seep, with wild, infracted course,
And restless roaring to the humble vale.
With the rough prospect tir'd, I turn my gaze,
Where, in long vista, the soft-murmuring main
Darts a green lustre, trembling thro' the trees;
Or to yon silver-streaming threads of light,
A showery radiance, beaming thro' the boughs.
Invited from the rock, to whose dark cliff
He clings, the steep-ascending eagle soars,
With upward pinions thro' th' attractive gleam:
And, giving full his bosom to the blaze,

And relatives endear'd for many a year,
Savag'd by woe, forget the social tye,
The close engagement of the kindred heart;
And, sick in solitude, successive die,
Untended, and unmourn'd. While to compleat
The scene of desolation, wide around,
Denying all retreat, the grim guards stand,
And give the flying wretch a better death.
Much of the force of foreign Summers still,
Of growling hills that shoot the pillar'd flame,
Of earthquake, and pale famine, could I sing;
But equal scenes of horror call me home.
For now, slow-settling, o'er the lurid grove,
Unusual darkness broods; and growing gains
The broad possession of the sky, surcharg'd
With wrathful vapour, from the damp abrupt,

Effusive source of evidence, and truth!
A lustre shedding o'er th' ennobled mind,
Stronger than summer-noon; and pure as that,
Whose mild vibrations sooth the parted soul,
New to the dawning of coelestial day.
Hence thro' her nourish'd powers, enlarg'd by thee,
She soaring spurns, with elevated pride,
The tangling mass of cares, and low desires,
That bind the fluttering croud; and, angel-wing'd,
The heights of Science, and of Virtue gains,
Where all is calm and clear; with Nature round
Or in the starry regions, or th' abyss,
To Reason's, and to fancy's eye display'd:
The First up-tracing from the vast inane,
The chain of causes and effects to Him,
Who, all-sustaining, in himself, alone

When, strict enquiring, from herself he found
She was the same, the daughter of his friend,
The bountiful Acasto; who can speak
The mingling passion that surpriz'd his heart,
And thro' his nerves in shivering transport ran?
Then blaz'd his smother'd flame, avowed, and bold;
And as he run her, ardent, o'er and o'er,
Love, gratitude, and pity wept at once.
Confus'd, and frighten'd at his sudden tears,
Her rising beauties flush'd a higher bloom,
As thus Palaemon, passionate, and just,
Pour'd out the pious rapture of his soul.
And art thou then Acasto's dear remains?
She, whom my restless gratitude has sought
So long in vain? Oh yes! the very same,
The soften'd image of my noble friend,

Quick o'er the kindling cheek the ready blush;
And from the smallest violence to shrink,
Unequal, then the loveliest in their fears;
And by this silent adulation, soft,
To their protection more engaging man.
O may their eyes no miserable sight,
Save weeping lovers, see! a nobler game,
Thro' love's enchanting wiles pursu'd, yet fled,
In chace ambiguous. May their tender limbs
Float in the loose simplicity of dress!
And fashion'd all to harmony, alone,
Know they to seize the captivated soul,
In rapture warbled from the radiant lip;
To teach the lute to languish; with smooth step,
Disclosing motion in its every charm,
To swim along, and swell the mazy dance;

Shade deepening over shade, the country round
Imbrown; a crowded umbrage, dusk, and dun,
Of every hue, from wan, declining green
To sooty dark. These now the lonesome muse,
Low-whispering, lead into their leaf-strown walks,
And give the Season in its latest view.
Mean-time, light-shadowing all, a sober calm
Fleeces unbounded ether; whose least wave
Stands tremulous, uncertain where to turn
The gentle current: while illumin'd wide,
The dewy-skirted clouds imbibe the sun,
And thro' their uvid pores his temper'd force
Shed o'er the peaceful world. Then is the time,
For those whom Wisdom, and whom Nature charm,
To steal themselves from the degenerate crowd,
And soar above this little scene of things;

And not an opening blossom breathes in vain.
In Summer he, beneath the living shade,
Such as from frigid Tempe wont to fall,
Or Haemus cool, reads what the muse, of these
Perhaps, has in immortal numbers sung;
Or what she dictates writes; and, oft an eye
Shot round, rejoyces in the vigorous year.
When Autumn's yellow lustre gilds the world,
And tempts the sickled swain into the field,
Seiz'd by the general joy, his heart distends
With gentle throws; and thro' the tepid gleams
Deep-musing, then the best exerts his song.
Even Winter wild to him is full of bliss.
The mighty tempest, and the hoary waste,
Abrupt, and deep, stretch'd o'er the bury'd earth,
Awake to solemn thought. At night the skies,

Of horrid prospect, shag the trackless plain:
Nor finds the river, nor the forest, hid
Beneath the white abrupt; but wanders on
From hill to dale, still more and more astray:
Impatient flouncing thro' the drifted heaps,
Stung with the thoughts of home; the thoughts of home
Rush on his nerves, and call their vigour forth

11. Aureolus. This man too, governing the Illyrican armies in contempt of Gallienus, as did all at that time, compelled by the soldiers, assumed the empire; and when Macrianus, with his son Macrianus, came against Gallienus with very many men, he captured his army, and bound some, corrupted, to his own allegiance. And when he had become from this a strong emperor, and Gallienus had vainly tried to overcome the brave man, he made peace with him, intending to fight against Postumus. Of which most things both have been and will be said. This same Aureolus Claudius—Gallienus having already been killed and a battle joined—slew at that bridge which is now called the Bridge of Aureolus; and there, as a tyrant, he gave him a rather humble tomb. There exists even now a Greek epigram in this form: "By the gift of a tomb, victor after many battles of the tyrant, Claudius, now fortunate, attends Aureolus with a mortal gift, and by right surviving him whom he would wish to live, if the love of an excellent soldiery allowed—which by right denied life to all the unworthy, and most of all to Aureolus. Yet he, merciful, preserving the last rites of the body, both dedicates the Bridge of Aureolus and the mound." These verses, translated by a certain grammarian, I have set down so as to keep faith—not that they could not have been better translated, but that historical fidelity might be preserved, which I have thought ought to be guarded above all else; for as to what pertains to eloquence, I care nothing. For I have proposed to deliver to you the matter, not the words—especially with so great an abundance of matters as in the Lives of thirty pretenders at once.
